# Message 1
## Tl;dr

1. We're working on a ticket to upgrade python and all the dependencies in the main branch of `es-as` and `es-hf`.  
    
2. We can basically just flip a switch and do this now without much effort. (We know because we did this 18 months ago when we were first learning about `es-hf`.)  
    
3. However, we can't upgrade beyond Python 3.11 unless we're willing to kill the `tflite-runtime` dependency of both repos and replace it with something else. There are two options for how to do this and both are easy.

Ok so...

If you (the reader) are ok with us doing thing 3, you're in luck: You can stop reading now! Hooray! Happy November. 🎉

Else if anyone has any reason to think we shouldn't do thing 3 in main, then the rest of the message is for you. 

It's all the details about why we can't upgrade stuff without doing that, and what the options for replacing it are.

---

**Version Upgrades, and Why They're Either Easy Or Impossible and We Get To Choose Which**

Background: About a year and a half ago, when we were first trying to learn how `es-hf` worked, we used the time-honored tradition of "deleting as much as possible without breaking stuff," in a new branch called `simple`, and then I made a movie documenting the step-by-step journey from the original codebase to the smallest working version whose outputs were the same as the original, mostly as a maybe-useful onboarding type thing, since it showed the type of stuff we ran into as noobs trying to understand the repo.

The version upgrade we're currently tasked with turned out to be one of the things we made to work back then, more or less just by deleting stuff.

The movie concluded with a run of the `main` vs `simple` branches on all the data we had at the time (full Neda2) and showed that the outputs were: (a) nearly always identical to around 8 decimal places, and (b) the max difference in any output in the million plus rows before and after the version upgrade and large refactor was ~ 0.001.

Note before we continue: I'm 99% sure that the small differences above are not due to the large refactor of the `es-hf` codebase between the `main` and `simple` branches. Those tiny changes are almost certainly due to upgrading python and its dependencies. None of the logic in the refactor is likely to have changed any float in the 8th decimal place. Some speed improvement deep inside (say) numpy easily could.

Now, while the process of creating `simple` was really helpful for us to get a better understanding of the `es-hf` repo, it ended up being a sufficiently large refactor that it was also pretty unfamiliar to folks who knew the repo (i.e., all of `es-hf` ended up in basically one file by the end, plus a short `pyproject.toml` and a few bits of glue) so we ended up not using the `simple` branch for anything except our own personal attempts to understand the repo's main branch, since their behavior was as close to identical as one could reasonably hope for.

Ok so, fast forward to now.

**Foreground:** In the past couple weeks, folks have mentioned the idea of doing a python version upgrade, and we're in charge of that ticket.

So, here's the deal.

Google has sort of unofficially deprecated all of tensorflow.

For details, see [here](https://developers.googleblog.com/whats-new-in-tensorflow-221 "https://developers.googleblog.com/whats-new-in-tensorflow-221") at the bottom. That post is from about eight months ago, but they've been heading in that direction for years.

The soft deprecation of tensorflow is relevant to the version upgrade because both the `es-as` and `es-hf` models use `tflite_runtime`, which is (a) a spinoff of the same project, and (b) even more deprecated than Tensorflow.

The latest release of `tflite_runtime` on PyPI was [3 years ago](https://pypi.org/project/tflite-runtime/#files "https://pypi.org/project/tflite-runtime/#files"), for Python 3.11.

That means we can't proceed with the version upgrade of python or anything else _unless_ we're willing to kill that library.

(Nostalgic note: This was one of the first things I spent time yammering about when we first got here, since it would be an easy win for not much effort if we're willing to do that.)

Fortunately, there's a fork of it that's still actively developed.

In the same Google post linked above, they say:

> Note: The TF Lite project has been renamed to [LiteRT](https://ai.google.dev/edge/litert "https://ai.google.dev/edge/litert") and is in active development separately.
> 
> While TensorFlow continues to provide stability for production, we recommend exploring our latest updates for Keras3, JAX, and PyTorch for new work in Generative AI.

So basically:

1. Google is saying "Don't use tensorflow for new projects."
2. That's ok. We're just upgrading versions for old projects.
3. However, an important dependency of both `es-as` and `es-hf` can't survive any python version upgrade past 3.11.
4. Fortunately, if we're willing to make some minor qualitative changes (e.g., use either `tensorflow.lite` (which `simple` did) or `litert` (the fork) instead of `tflite_runtime`, then it's possible to upgrade the python version and the versions of all dependencies with almost no work or headaches.
5. If we're willing to do that, the biggest time requirement will literally just be typing this message. The rest is easy.

Bigger picture:

1. We have several options for how to do the version upgrade.
2. All the options are easy, since we've done this or something 99% like it before.
3. None of the possibilities involve keeping `tflite-runtime`.
4. One of the two options is something we've already done a full before and after analysis of and shown that the differences were negligible.

At this point we can do another `if / else` statement to let you stop reading if you're convinced, so...

If everyone's cool with the thing now: Hooray we're done you can stop reading! 🎉

Else if not, follow me and let's dig deeper into the details down below.

## The Options

**Option 1: The thing we did 18 months ago.**

Do what the `simple` branch did. It's already a version of `es-hf` running:

- On python 3.13.
- With the latest versions of all dependencies.
- With `tflite_runtime` replaced by `tensorflow.lite`.

Though `tensorflow` isn't being actively developed anymore, it's still getting security fixed and bug fixed, and there's a version [here](https://pypi.org/project/tensorflow/2.22.0rc0/#files "https://pypi.org/project/tensorflow/2.22.0rc0/#files") that works with python 3.14.

**Option 2: Use a library called** `**litert**`

We haven't tried this approach yet, but this project is actively developed, and _may_ be more similar to `tflite_runtime` since I assume it's mostly being developed for backward compatability reasons, i.e., for folks like us.

Leaving aside the large refactor in `simple` and just focusing on the subset of changes we'd need to do the version upgrade, basically all we have to do is replace the file on the left with the one on the right:

![image](data:image/webp;base64,)

If we just want to focus on the version-upgrade-related stuff, all we have to do is replace the hard-coded versions here:

![image](data:image/webp;base64,)

with the simpler version here:

![image](data:image/webp;base64,)

And then everything magically works with (a) lots of different python versions, and (b) the latest version of all dependencies, except in rare cases where we run into an actual issue and need to say "no" to the buggy version, e.g., the `tensorflow < 2.20` example above.

In other words, "version upgrades" already happen automatically.

We just need to remove the bit of the repo that makes it not happen.

If you're STILL here, then (a) wow, (b) I'm impressed, (c) you're a very patient person, and (d) you're probably not hating reading this, cuz if you were I'd assume you'd have taken one of the exits we placed up above, so therefore (e) we may as well finish up with The Big Picture of what we can learn from this whole (otherwise pretty mundane) process of version upgrades, cuz it's a cool example of how reality is often the exact opposite of our intuitions, even about stuff we do as a job, like software.

_(ahem)_

**Why this is actually "best practices" even if it feels like the opposite:**

(Note: the word "this" up there is short for "deleting the hard-coded version numbers from requirements files, both for the dependencies and for python itself.")

1. If you look at most successful large open source projects (e.g., the dependencies in that list: numpy, pandas, sklearn, hundreds of others), this is what they all do with the versions of pretty much all dependencies (except external dev tools like linters, for example.)  
    
2. The OS with the largest package repository in the world (NixOS) actually has code in its package manager to rip out the hard-coded `pkg==a.b.c` requirements out of every python package in the python ecosystem, since those requirements (a) are fragile, (b) don't compose, and (c) aren't real (i.e., they virtually never reflect an actual requirement, they just feel like the safer choice so they end up in lots of projects and then have to be removed by distro maintainers or anyone who builds a large working system.)  
    
3. Even in production environments, the right way to increase stability by "freezing versions" is not by using the `==` to pin versions. If a product needs to be shipped into a runtime environment where it can't easily receive bugfixes or security updates over time, then the right way to "freeze versions" in order to increase stability is to just ship all the product's dependencies along with it, inside the container or whatever the execution environment is. Using the `==` _feels_ like it's doing that. It's not. It's placing strong demands on _future_ downloads and failing on purpose if anything changes, in precisely the environment we've postulated we can't easily ship bugfixes into. Using `==` in a python codebase commonly leads to products whose Dockerfile or other setup does something like a `pip install` of the requirements at runtime, and if the requirements contain `==` or the narrow version ranges that tools like poetry default to, then as the years pass, the product ends up making an increasingly hard-to-satisfy set of demands on infrastructure in the outside world, e.g., PyPI, or assorted backend APIs with URLs that may not exist anymore but which still exist in the pinned version of a package the product depends on. Example: huggingface transformers has the ability to download terabytes of models, so naturally it just downloads them on demand, from urls that aren't guaranteed to be the same in the future, but at all times the package will contain whatever urls the site is using, because huggingface controls both. So, every time you see a troubleshooting thread where the dev's solution is "Upgrade to the latest version," you've just seen a reason why any code that pinned an older version will break. Etc. etc. this makes maintenance more expensive for companies and makes life sadder and makes Jason type long things he shouldn't have typed. I'm gonna be done now. End of thing.

Oh also, if you got this message but you're on that other team of dev folks, it's because I found your name in the git log for those two repos doing stuff like version updates and security stuff.

**_Quick explanation about why This Is The Way in python specifically, but not necessarily in other languages, cuz other languages do this whole "I need package X" thing differently:_**

There ARE languages where you can have a dependency hierarchy where every level of the import hierarchy does version pinning, but python isn't one of them.

When that's possible, it's usually compiled languages that can solve the diamond problem² through some black magic related to name mangling at the linker level.¹

[Inline Footnote 1: Please ignore this sentence if it doesn't make sense. It's too nerdy. But it's late here so my brain is insisting I keep it in. Apologies on its behalf.]

[Inline Footnote 2: Diamond problem. (noun). That thing where package A depends on B and C which both depend on D but they pin different versions of D so you need the language to support two versions of D at runtime within a single process. Now see footnote 1 because the "This is too nerdy, apologies" comment up there applies here too.]
